extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (IPR petitioners and patent owners), patent attorneys, and patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Applying claim construction and prior-art comparison in an inter partes review to determine whether prior art teaches each claim limitation (including subsidiary dependent-claim limitations) and whether arguments or evidence are forfeited or discredited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'for use in a mobile video game' / 'usable in the video game' / 'video-game content being usable when the video game operates'
rubrics_metrics.description: These phrases do not require an interactive object or new ad unit that is inserted into an existing game that alters the functionality of the game.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclosure that uploads advertisements to a mobile communications device and presents those advertisements in ad units within that game during game play can satisfy these phrases—ads displayed as skins or as items used by game characters (e.g., a brand name soft drink or energy bar) are 'usable' by the game and by the player. The presence of examples of interactive ad units (e.g., a character eating an energy bar to boost power) supports finding content is 'usable when the video game operates.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-art teaching of claim limitation via disclosure of inserted agents/bots
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art disclosure that the advertisement management service 'may send bots or electronic agents into the game as advertising units or real characters' teaches inserting content beyond mere skins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the prior art describes sending bots/agents into a game (not merely changing skins on preexisting geometry), that supports finding the prior art teaches insertion of updated content usable in the game (e.g., a bot offering a branded drink implies the player's character may interact/use it). Conflicting expert testimony that contradicts the disclosure may be disregarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching 'checking what updated video-game content to send' based on factors including device type/service provider
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitation [1b] requires 'checking what updated video-game content to send based on one of the factors including a type of the mobile communication device, a telecom service associated with the mobile communication device, and a service provider of the telecom service.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior-art system that includes a client-type field (e.g., SKU indicating 'cellular or mobile phones') and an advertising matching/weighting system that derives weights from that client type teaches 'checking' based on device type. Demographic data like IP addresses, when tied to a cellular service provider, can correspond to 'service provider' factors. It is sufficient if the selection/weights are at least partly based on such factors even if additional internal weighting/comparisons between ads occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting/matching that uses client/device factors qualifies as 'checking' step
rubrics_metrics.description: A weighting and matching routine that assigns weights to advertisements derived from client-type information counts as checking what to send based on device-related factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the system subsequently compares weighted advertisements to each other, the fact that advertisement weights are derived from client/device factors means the system 'checks' based on those factors. The existence of an extra comparison stage between ads does not negate that the selection was based on device factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-step ordering not presumed unless claim language requires it
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that claim steps must occur in a specific order are forfeited if not raised earlier; and the claim language, not extrinsic assumptions, determines required order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim explicitly recites an order (e.g., 'receiving... then checking... then uploading'), that order may be given effect; however, a prior-art disclosure describing a request followed by matching/weighting and then sending content can satisfy ordered steps. New arguments about order raised for the first time late may be forfeited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim term 'mobile communications device' scope is not limited to cellular phones
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Mobile communications devices' can include consoles, PDAs, and other handheld devices capable of communication with a server; they are not limited to wireless-only devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a device is capable of communicating with a server (regardless of transport), it can fall within 'mobile communications device.' Thus, prior-art disclosures of consoles or other devices capable of server communication can fall within the claimed scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony inconsistent with the intrinsic record is given little or no weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony from an expert that is plainly inconsistent with the prior-art disclosure or the specification should not be credited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite authorities (e.g., Homeland Housewares v. Whirlpool) and compare expert assertions to specific paragraphs of the prior art. If the record shows the opposite, the expert's contrary statements are discounted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture of arguments not raised in initial Patent Owner Response
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments introduced for the first time in a sur-reply (or later filing) that were not presented in the Patent Owner Response may be considered forfeited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite applicable precedent (e.g., In re Google Tech.). New theories or fact-based arguments raised for the first time late in briefing are subject to forfeiture and may not be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent-claim limitations analyzed individually against prior art (claims 2–9 examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each dependent claim limitation (e.g., promotional content; technical media format checks; predetermined display period; location-based selection; demographic targeting) must be shown in the prior art to find that claim taught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision evaluates dependent limitations separately: claim 2 (promotional content) is shown by branded in-game items; claim 3 (technical media formats/approval) by client-specific accepted media formats and approvals; claim 7 (display for predetermined period) by campaigns tied to seasons/dates/times; claim 8 (location-based selection) by GPS-based targeting; claim 9 (demographic targeting) by age/sex/location/purchasing-habit targeting. If the prior art includes examples or paragraphs disclosing these features, that supports teaching of the dependent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sending information that provides an in-game placement location as part of updated content (claim 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim 4 requires 'sending information to the mobile communication device as part of the updated content, the information providing an in-game placement location associated with the updated video-game content.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A server that sends lists of advertisements 'for specific available ad units' or specifies which advertisements are for which ad units teaches sending placement-location information. Even if advertisers create standardized ads, when the server sends ad lists for specific ad units or insertion orders specify ad unit placement, the logical implication is that placement information is sent as part of the updated content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracking what has been uploaded to the mobile communication device (claim 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim 5 recites 'the step of tracking what has been uploaded to the mobile communication device.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of an active session database that 'registers the game player... and is used to track and record all communications and data sent to and received from the advertisement recipient client' teaches tracking what has been uploaded. The claim language does not require tracking everything uploaded; tracking a portion of uploaded content (or all communications within sessions) can be sufficient if the specification describes such tracking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displaying updated video-game content at a location based on user interaction (claim 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim 6 requires that uploading comprises 'displaying the video-game content within the game at a location based on user interaction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples where a bot offers an item to a player, or ad units tied to particular storefronts/panels that appear when the player's character arrives at those locations, support that the displayed content's location is based on user interaction (e.g., player's character location or session continuity). Prior-art descriptions that the location of displayed adverts is determined by the player's character position or interaction support this limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia/teaching-away arguments require evidentiary support and are weakened by unsupported expert assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that the prior art 'taught away' or that particular implementations were infeasible due to bandwidth/storage/processing must be supported by factual evidence; unsupported expert testimony carries little weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An expert's conclusory statements about technical infeasibility are entitled to little weight if they do not identify the basis for the testimony. General statements that prior art taught away must be tied to specific disclosures or contemporaneous technical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'tracking' need not mean comprehensive coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting 'tracking what has been uploaded' does not necessarily require tracking everything uploaded to the device in its entirety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the claim language is broad or ambiguous, evidence that the prior art tracks at least a portion of uploaded content (e.g., all communications during a session) can meet the limitation. An opponent's argument that only partial tracking is disclosed may fail if the specification states tracking of 'all communications and data' for sessions.
